The letter arrived on the first of July, on heavy cream-coloured paper, with the red lily crest at the top left. Graziella opened it in the kitchen, her hands still covered in flour, and read it aloud, slowly, the way you read an important document: "Dear Signora Graziella, we are pleased to inform you that the Trattoria in Via Maggio has been entered in the Register of Historic Shops of the City of Florence. We therefore invite you to the plaque presentation ceremony, which will take place on Saturday 11 July at 11 a.m. in the Salone dei Cinquecento of Palazzo Vecchio. Yours faithfully."

When she had finished there was a silence. Then Lorenzo, the baker's grandson, who had come by with the bread and stopped to listen, said what everyone was thinking: "That's so cool! The Salone dei Cinquecento! That's where they do the serious stuff, like when the president comes." Graziella looked at him over her glasses. "Lorenzo, you don't say 'so cool' in front of ladies." "Sorry, Signora Graziella," said Lorenzo, blushing. "I meant: what an extraordinary honour." Everyone laughed, Graziella included.

The real problem was the speech. At the end of the letter, in small print, it said that "the proprietor of the establishment is invited to deliver a brief address of thanks". Graziella read the sentence three times. "What does 'establishment' mean?" she asked. "It means the trattoria," explained Valeria Conti, who by now dropped into Via Maggio almost every evening. "And 'a brief address of thanks' means you have to say thank you. In two minutes." Graziella put the letter down. "Two minutes? In front of the mayor? Me? I reckon this time ribollita won't be enough."

For a week the trattoria became a school of registers. Valeria taught the formal register: how to greet a mayor, how to thank people without sounding servile, how to use "Lei" even when you're nervous. Pietro, who had just finished primary school and now felt like an expert in communication, corrected everything that seemed to him "too bank-like". And Signor Franco, who came by every morning for his coffee, added a broad Florentine version to every sentence, "because otherwise people will think you're from Milan".

On the first day Graziella wrote: "Hi everyone, thanks for coming, I can't make speeches, so eat." Valeria found it sincere but impossible. On the second day, on Valeria's advice, she wrote a whole page that began "Dear Mr Mayor, Most Illustrious Authorities, Ladies and Gentlemen" and ended "in the hope of having proved myself worthy of the honour conferred upon me". Pietro read it and said: "Grandma, you sound like a robot that works in a bank." On the third day Graziella threw everything away and wrote nothing.

It was Bellini, on the fourth day, who gave her the right advice. He was sitting at his usual table with his coffee, watching her cross out the same sentence for the tenth time. "Graziella," he said, "do you know how an old painting is restored? You don't redo it all from scratch. You only remove the dirt and leave what was underneath." Graziella looked up. "And so?" "And so you already have your speech. You say it every day to your customers. Just take out the swear words and add 'Mr Mayor' at the beginning."

Meanwhile, in the rest of the family, registers were mixing cheerfully. Davide, who had come to show Pietro the drawing of the plaque he had done for the paper, said it was "a bloody brilliant drawing", and Graziella told him off. Chiara, on the phone with a paint supplier, went in ten seconds from "Good morning, would you be so kind as to check my order?" to "What do you mean it hasn't arrived? It's a disaster, I've got an altar to finish!". And Viola, who at two imitated everything, had learned from Lorenzo to say "figo", and said it about everything: the cake, Lupino, the mayor on television.

The day before the ceremony, Pietro had a task all of his own. Valeria had explained that a formal letter had to be sent to the city to say who would accompany the proprietor. Pietro wrote it himself on the workshop computer and had everyone read it before sending it. "Dear Protocol Office, we hereby inform you that Signora Graziella will be accompanied by six family members, a professor, a journalist, an artist and a dog. The dog is well-behaved. Awaiting your kind reply, we send you our kind regards."

The Protocol Office replied the next morning, with great courtesy, that unfortunately dogs were not allowed in the Salone dei Cinquecento, "with the exception of guide dogs". Pietro replied at once that Lupino was, in a sense, a guide dog, because he guided the whole family to the kitchen when it was time to eat. The Office did not reply again. Lupino stayed at home with Signor Franco, who didn't like ceremonies and said he preferred to watch it on television, "so if the mayor talks too much, I can change the channel".

On the morning of the ceremony, while Graziella was getting dressed, Signor Franco gave Pietro his last lesson in Florentine, sitting at the counter with his coffee. "Right, repeat after me," he said. "You don't say 'che cosa fai?', you say 'icché tu fai?'. You don't say 'la mia mamma', you say 'la mi' mamma'. And above all, the 'c' in the middle of words isn't pronounced: 'casa' becomes 'la hasa', and 'Coca-Cola' becomes 'la hoha-hola'." Pietro tried. What came out was something between Florentine and a head cold. Franco shook his head gravely. "Forget it," he concluded. "You were born here, but you talk like the television. It's the school's fault. In my day the teacher in class talked like my grandmother." Then he patted him on the shoulder. "But you corrected your grandmother's speech well. Now that is Florentine: saying things as they are, and quickly, because the soup is waiting."

On Saturday 11 July the Salone dei Cinquecento was full. Beneath the enormous battle frescoes, on red velvet chairs, sat the owners of twelve historic shops: a goldsmith from the Ponte Vecchio, a seventeenth-century pharmacy, a violin maker, an antiquarian bookshop, a blacksmith, a pastry shop. The trattoria in Via Maggio was last on the list. Graziella wore her blue dress for special occasions, the one she had worn for Viola's baptism, and held a slip of paper with three lines written in pencil.

The mayor spoke for a quarter of an hour, in perfect and slightly boring Italian, about "safeguarding intangible heritage", the "social fabric" and "urban identity". Pietro, sitting in the second row, was taking notes for Mancini, who had asked him to write an article for the children's page. Next to "intangible heritage" he wrote in brackets: "= the beautiful things you can't touch, like ribollita (which you can eat, though)". Davide, next to him, was drawing the mayor with slightly bigger ears than in real life.

Then they called Graziella. She went up onto the stage, received from the mayor's hands a brass plaque reading "Historic Shop of Florence — since 1952", looked at it for a long time and stepped up to the microphone. She opened the slip of paper. Her hands were trembling a little. Bellini, in the third row, closed his eyes as he did when waiting for the result of an X-ray. Matei held Viola tight, ready to cover her mouth if she said "figo" at the wrong moment.

"Mr Mayor," Graziella began in a steady voice, "I thank you. I thank Councillor Neri, Ms Conti and everyone who signed, wrote, drew and protested." Then she folded the slip of paper, put it in her pocket and went on without reading. "I can't make speeches. My dad used to say words are like salt: just a few, otherwise you ruin the soup. So I'll just tell you this. He opened the trattoria in 1952, with my mum. I grew up in it. My husband ate ribollita there for a year before he had the courage to speak to me. And my grandson made his first speech there, standing on a chair."

"This plaque," she said, raising it a little, "I'll put next to the door. But I'll tell you something: the historic shop isn't the wall, and it isn't the recipe either. It's the people who come in. As long as they come in, the trattoria is there. And now, Mr Mayor, I do beg your pardon, but it's nearly noon, and in Via Maggio the ribollita's getting cold. You're all invited." There was a moment's silence, then the Salone dei Cinquecento, which had heard speeches by kings, popes and presidents, burst into applause. The mayor was laughing. And Viola, in the silence that followed, said loud and clear: "Figo!"

The mayor really did come to eat ribollita in Via Maggio that day. He sat at the table by the window, took off his jacket, and after his second plate said to Graziella, in a Florentine he hadn't used during the whole ceremony: "Signora, what d'you put in it? Don't tell me you won't say." Graziella smiled. "Mr Mayor," she replied, going back to the most formal "Lei" she knew, "I'm sorry, but the recipe is intangible heritage. You can eat it, but you can't take it away."

That evening, when everyone had left, Marco screwed the brass plaque next to the trattoria door. Pietro held the ladder, Graziella gave orders from the pavement: "More to the right. No, more to the left. There. No, it was better before." In the end the plaque was in place, slightly crooked, just under the old hand-painted sign. Graziella looked at it for a long time, arms folded. Then she said, in the most informal register in the world, the one you use only with people you love: "Dad, look. We did it."

The next day was 12 July, Pietro's birthday. Twelve years old. Before the cake, as every year, Marco stood him with his back against the door frame of Viola's little room, where the whole family's notches were, and marked his new height in pencil. It was higher than Marco's at twelve. Pietro looked at the notch, then at his dad, and said, in the register that came most naturally to him: "Gotcha, Dad. I'm taller than you." Marco laughed. "Not yet," he replied. "But I reckon it won't be long."
